runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I
This chapter explains how computers find each other on a network, and how you check, set and change a Linux server's network settings. You learn addresses and routes, test commands, the
tool, the configuration files behind it, and host names and name lookup.
Configuring Networking from the Command Line
Configuring Host Names and Name Resolution
The TCP/IP model describes how computers send data over a network, using four layers.

is an agreed set of rules for communicating. Sending data is like sending a letter: write it, pick a delivery service, address the envelope, put it on a truck. Each layer does one job and hands the data to the next. The comparison stops here: the layers work together automatically.
The model is described in RFC 1122.

1.5 Setting IPv4 addresses: DHCP or static
A server gets its IPv4 settings either automatically from a DHCP server or from local files.

configuration, the settings come from local files. You must get correct values from your network administrator and update them by hand, so they do not clash with other servers. DHCP is like a hotel assigning a room; static is owning the house.
DHCP = automatic lease; static = you set it and you keep it correct.

A RHEL 8 machine that gets IPv4 by DHCP is usually also set to use SLAAC for IPv6. It can unexpectedly get an IPv6 address when an IPv6 router is added to the network. Some sites combine SLAAC (addresses) with DHCPv6 (other data such as DNS servers and search domains).
